claim: Ionotropic Receptors (IRs) are a large subfamily of variant ionotropic glutamate receptors present across Protostomia.
source: Ionotropic Receptors (IRs) are a large subfamily of variant ionotropic glutamate receptors present across Protostomia.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work establishing IRs as a subfamily of ionotropic glutamate receptors found across Protostomia.

claim: IR21a and IR25a are implicated in thermosensation in Drosophila.
source: recent work has implicated two family members, IR21a and IR25a, in thermosensation in Drosophila.
evidence: This claim references recent work that has shown these receptors function in thermosensation.

claim: IR93a is one of the most evolutionarily deeply conserved receptors.
source: Here we characterize one of the most evolutionarily deeply conserved receptors, IR93a
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the evolutionary conservation of IR93a.

claim: IR93a is co-expressed and functions with IR21a and IR25a to mediate physiological and behavioral responses to cool temperatures.
source: Here we characterize one of the most evolutionarily deeply conserved receptors, IR93a, and show that it is co-expressed and functions with IR21a and IR25a to mediate physiological and behavioral responses to cool temperatures.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing co-expression and functional requirements.

claim: IR93a is co-expressed with IR25a and IR40a in a discrete population of sensory neurons in the sacculus.
source: IR93a is also co-expressed with IR25a and a distinct receptor, IR40a, in a discrete population of sensory neurons in the sacculus, a multi-chambered pocket within the antenna.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing co-expression patterns.

claim: The combination of IR93a, IR25a, and IR40a is required for neuronal responses to dry air.
source: We demonstrate that this combination of receptors is required for neuronal responses to dry air and behavioral discrimination of humidity differences.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data showing loss of dry air responses in mutants.

claim: The combination of IR93a, IR25a, and IR40a is required for behavioral discrimination of humidity differences.
source: We demonstrate that this combination of receptors is required for neuronal responses to dry air and behavioral discrimination of humidity differences.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral assay data showing loss of humidity preference in mutants.

claim: IR93a is a common component of molecularly and cellularly distinct IR pathways important for thermosensation and hygrosensation in insects.
source: Our results identify IR93a as a common component of molecularly and cellularly distinct IR pathways important for thermosensation and hygrosensation in insects.
evidence: This claim is based on the data showing IR93a functions in both thermosensation (with IR21a) and hygrosensation (with IR40a).

claim: IRs appear to have evolved in the last common protostome ancestor.
source: Ionotropic Receptors (IRs) are a large subfamily of ionotropic glutamate receptors (iGluRs) that appear to have evolved in the last common protostome ancestor (Benton et al., 2009; Croset et al., 2010; Rytz et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous phylogenetic analyses.

claim: IRs have diverse roles in chemosensory detection.
source: In contrast to the critical role of iGluRs in synaptic communication, IRs have diverse roles in chemosensory detection (Koh et al., 2014; Rytz et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work characterizing IR functions.

claim: IRs mediate sensory neuron responses to diverse chemicals, including many acids and amines.
source: The best-defined functions of IRs are in olfaction, where they mediate sensory neuron responses to diverse chemicals, including many acids and amines (Rytz et al., 2013; Silbering et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous functional studies.

claim: Most IRs are thought to form heteromeric ligand-gated ion channels.
source: Most IRs are thought to form heteromeric ligand-gated ion channels, in which broadly expressed co-receptor subunits (e.g., IR8a, IR25a and IR76b) combine with more selectively expressed IR subunits that confer stimulus specificity (Abuin et al., 2011; Rytz et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on previous studies characterizing IR structure and function.

claim: Many IRs are highly conserved in insects.
source: Many of these IRs are highly conserved in insects, indicating that they define sensory pathways common to a wide range of species (Croset et al., 2010; Rytz et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to comparative genomic studies.

claim: IR21a mediates cool sensing together with IR25a in the dorsal organ cool cells (DOCCs) of Drosophila melanogaster larvae.
source: Although most conserved IRs have been assigned chemosensory roles, we recently reported that one of these receptors, IR21a, mediates cool sensing (together with IR25a) in a population of neurons in the Drosophila melanogaster larva, the dorsal organ cool cells (DOCCs) (Ni et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: IR93a has orthologs across arthropods.
source: In this work we characterize one of these 'orphan' receptors, IR93a, which has orthologs across arthropods (Corey et al., 2013; Groh-Lunow et al., 2014; Rytz et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to comparative genomic studies.

claim: IR93a receptor gene is transcribed in peripheral sensory organs in several insects and crustaceans.
source: RNA expression analysis in several insects and crustaceans indicates that this receptor gene is transcribed in peripheral sensory organs (Benton et al., 2009; Corey et al., 2013; Groh-Lunow et al., 2014; Rytz et al., 2013), but its role(s) are unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous expression studies.

claim: IR93a acts with different combinations of IRs in distinct populations of neurons to mediate physiological and behavioral responses to both thermosensory and hygrosensory cues.
source: Using Drosophila as a model, we find that IR93a acts with different combinations of IRs in distinct populations of neurons to mediate physiological and behavioral responses to both thermosensory and hygrosensory cues.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ir93aMI05555 contains a transposon insertion in the fifth coding exon.
source: Ir93aMI05555, which contains a transposon insertion in the fifth coding exon
evidence: This claim is supported by the gene structure diagram in Figure 1a.

claim: Ir93a122 was generated using CRISPR/Cas9 to delete 22 bases within the sequence encoding the first transmembrane domain.
source: Ir93a122, which we generated using CRISPR/Cas9 to delete 22 bases within the sequence encoding the first transmembrane domain (Figure 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by the gene structure diagram and sequence information in Figure 1a.

claim: IR93a protein is expressed in several neurons in the dorsal organ ganglion in larvae.
source: In larvae, IR93a protein is expressed in several neurons in the dorsal organ ganglion, one of the main sensory organs in the larval head (Stocker, 1994) (Figure 1b–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: IR93a-expressing neurons in larvae encompass the DOCCs.
source: These neurons encompass the DOCCs (labeled by an Ir21a promoter-Gal4-driven GFP reporter)
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: IR93a protein localizes prominently to the dendritic bulb at the tip of the sensory processes of DOCCs.
source: and the protein localizes prominently to the dendritic bulb at the tip of the sensory processes of these cells (Figure 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 1c.

claim: All IR93a expression was absent in Ir93a mutants.
source: All expression was absent in Ir93a mutants, confirming antiserum specificity (Figure 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing loss of signal in mutants in Figure 1c.

claim: Both Ir93a mutant alleles exhibited strong defects in cool avoidance when larval thermotaxis was assessed on a thermal gradient.
source: Indeed, when larval thermotaxis was assessed on a thermal gradient (Klein et al., 2015), we found both Ir93a mutant alleles exhibited strong defects in cool avoidance (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Cell-specific expression of an Ir93a cDNA in the DOCCs under Ir21a-Gal4 control fully rescued the cool avoidance mutant phenotype.
source: Cell-specific expression of an Ir93a cDNA in the DOCCs under Ir21a-Gal4 control fully rescued this mutant phenotype (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral rescue data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: IR93a has an essential role in DOCCs in larval thermotaxis.
source: These data demonstrate an essential role for IR93a in DOCCs in larval thermotaxis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the mutant and rescue data presented.

claim: Wild-type DOCCs exhibit robust increases in intracellular calcium in response to cooling.
source: As previously reported (Klein et al., 2015; Ni et al., 2016), wild-type DOCCs exhibit robust increases in intracellular calcium in response to cooling (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2a and citations to previous work.

claim: Calcium responses to cooling in DOCCs were dramatically reduced in Ir93a mutants.
source: These responses were dramatically reduced in Ir93a mutants, and could be rescued by cell-specific expression of an Ir93a cDNA (using the R11F02-Gal4 DOCC driver [Klein et al., 2015]) (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2a-b.

claim: The dramatic loss of DOCC temperature sensitivity in Ir93a mutants resembles that observed in both Ir21a and Ir25a mutants.
source: This dramatic loss of DOCC temperature sensitivity resembles that observed in both Ir21a and Ir25a mutants (Ni et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to previously published data.

claim: IR21a, IR25a and IR93a function together to mediate cool activation of the DOCCs.
source: and is consistent with IR21a, IR25a and IR93a functioning together to mediate cool activation of the DOCCs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the similar phenotypes of the three mutants.

claim: Mutations in either Ir93a or Ir40a eliminated the cool response in DOCC sensory endings.
source: This response was completely eliminated in Ir21a, Ir25a and Ir93a mutants (Figure 2c–e)
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage imaging data shown in Figure 2c-e.

claim: Each of IR21a, IR25a and IR93a is required for temperature-dependent voltage changes in the DOCC sensory compartment.
source: indicating that each of these IRs is required for temperature-dependent voltage changes in this sensory compartment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the voltage imaging data showing loss of responses in all three mutants.

claim: Ir93a transcripts were previously weakly detected in a set of neurons in the third antennal segment surrounding the sacculus in adults.
source: In adults, Ir93a transcripts were previously weakly detected in a set of neurons in the third antennal segment surrounding the sacculus, a three-chambered pouch whose opening lies on the posterior surface of the antenna (Benton et al., 2009) (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous expression data.

claim: IR93a is expressed in neurons innervating sacculus chamber I (11.0 ± 0.5 neurons, n = 48 animals).
source: With our IR93a antibody, we detected IR93a expression in neurons innervating sacculus chamber I (11.0 ± 0.5 neurons, n = 48 animals; mean ± SEM)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 3b.

claim: IR93a is expressed in neurons innervating sacculus chamber II (13.9 ± 0.7 neurons, n = 23 animals).
source: and chamber II (13.9 ± 0.7 neurons, n = 23)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data and quantification shown in Figure 3b.

claim: IR93a signal is detected both in the soma and in the sensory cilia that project into cuticular sensory hairs (sensilla) in adult sacculus neurons.
source: with signal detected both in the soma and in the sensory cilia that project into cuticular sensory hairs (sensilla) (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 3b.

claim: IR25a is expressed in IR93a-expressing cells in the sacculus.
source: As in larval DOCCs, IR25a was expressed in IR93a-expressing cells in the sacculus (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by double immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: No Ir21a promoter driver expression was detected in IR93a-expressing sacculus cells.
source: By contrast, no expression was detected in these cells when using our Ir21a promoter driver (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on negative data from expression analysis.

claim: The IR93a/IR25a sacculus neurons express IR40a.
source: We found instead that the IR93a/IR25a sacculus neurons express a distinct receptor, IR40a (Figure 3d–e) (Benton et al., 2009; Silbering et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by double immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3d-e.

claim: Morphological studies have suggested that neurons in sacculus chambers I and II are hygroreceptive.
source: Morphological studies have suggested that neurons in sacculus chambers I and II are hygroreceptive (Shanbhag et al., 1995)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous morphological work.

claim: Wild-type flies exhibited a strong preference for lower humidity in the hygrosensory behavior assay.
source: Consistent with previous observations (Perttunen and Salmi, 1956), wild-type flies exhibited a strong preference for lower humidity (Figure 4c).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4c and citation to previous work.

claim: The preference for lower humidity was completely eliminated in Ir93a and Ir25a mutant flies.
source: This preference was completely eliminated in Ir93a and Ir25a mutant flies
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The preference for lower humidity was significantly reduced, but not abolished, in Ir40a mutants.
source: and significantly reduced, but not abolished, in Ir40a mutants (Figure 4c, Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: All hygrosensory behavioral defects were robustly rescued by the corresponding cDNAs.
source: All of these behavioral defects were robustly rescued by the corresponding cDNAs, confirming the specificity of the mutant defects (Figure 4c).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral rescue data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The loss of Ir21a did not disrupt dry preference behavior.
source: Importantly, the loss of Ir21a (or other antennal-expressed IR co-receptors, Ir8a and Ir76b) did not disrupt dry preference.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Wild type flies displayed a strong preference for the side with lower humidity even in a very shallow gradient (~89% to ~96% RH).
source: Even in this very shallow gradient, wild type flies displayed a strong preference for the side with lower humidity (Figure 4d)
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The preference for lower humidity in the shallow gradient was dependent on IR93a, IR25a and IR40a, but independent of IR21a.
source: and this preference was dependent on IR93a, IR25a and IR40a, but independent of IR21a (Figure 4d).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Ir40a mutants exhibited no defects in thermotaxis.
source: The distinction between the functions of IR21a and IR40a extended to thermotaxis, as Ir40a mutants exhibited no defects in this IR21a-dependent behavior (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–b)
evidence: This claim is supported by thermotaxis behavioral data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a-b.

claim: IR40a is not expressed in the larval DOCCs.
source: consistent with lack of expression of IR40a in the larval DOCCs (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on negative expression data.

claim: IR40a/IR93a/IR25a-expressing sacculus neurons behave as dry-activated hygrosensors.
source: We observed that these sacculus neurons behave as dry-activated hygrosensors: decreasing the RH from ~90% to ~7% RH elicited an increase in GCaMP6m fluorescence, while increasing RH from ~7% to ~90% elicited a decrease (Figure 5c–g).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5c-g.

claim: Calcium changes in response to humidity were most apparent in the 'arm' region of the antennal lobe.
source: Calcium changes were most apparent in the 'arm' (Figure 5c).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Mutations in either Ir93a or Ir40a eliminated the dry response in sacculus neurons.
source: Importantly, these physiological responses were IR-dependent: mutations in either Ir93a or Ir40a eliminated the dry response (Ir25a mutants were not tested)
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5d-g.

claim: The hygrosensory physiological defects in Ir93a and Ir40a mutants were restored with corresponding cDNA rescue transgenes.
source: and these defects were restored with corresponding cDNA rescue transgenes (Figure 5d–g).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging rescue data shown in Figure 5d-g.

claim: Previous work has implicated two TRP channels, Nanchung and Water witch, in hygrosensation.
source: Previous work has implicated two Transient Receptor Potential (TRP) channels, Nanchung and Water witch, in hygrosensation (Liu et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: It is unclear whether Nanchung and Water witch have an essential function in hygrosensation.
source: but it is unclear whether they have an essential function in this modality (Enjin et al., 2016; Ji and Zhu, 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to conflicting previous work.

claim: The cells in which Nanchung and Water witch act are unknown.
source: and the cells in which these proteins act are unknown (Jourjine et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Animals mutant for nanchung or water witch displayed partially diminished dry preference behavior.
source: In our gradient assay, we found that animals mutant for nanchung or water witch displayed partially diminished dry preference behavior (Figure 6a).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Neither nan nor wtrw was required for the dry responsiveness of IR40a-expressing sacculus neurons.
source: However, neither nan nor wtrw was required for the dry responsiveness of IR40a-expressing sacculus neurons (Figure 6b–e).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6b-e.

claim: Nanchung and Water witch are not essential for IR-dependent dry sensing.
source: Thus, these TRP channels are not essential for IR-dependent dry sensing
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing normal IR40a neuron responses in nan and wtrw mutants.

claim: Nanchung and Water witch contribute to hygrotaxis through mechanisms other than IR-dependent dry sensing.
source: suggesting that they contribute to hygrotaxis through other mechanisms.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the behavioral defects without physiological defects in IR neurons.

claim: IRs have evolved functionally diverse roles in environmental chemosensory detection from their ancestral origins within the synaptic iGluR family.
source: From their ancestral origins within the synaptic iGluR family, IRs are widely appreciated to have evolved functionally diverse roles in environmental chemosensory detection (Croset et al., 2010; Rytz et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on IR evolution and function.

claim: IR93a functions in two critical non-chemosensory modalities, thermosensation and hygrosensation.
source: Here we provide evidence that a previously uncharacterized member of this repertoire, IR93a, functions in two critical non-chemosensory modalities, thermosensation and hygrosensation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In both thermosensation and hygrosensation roles, IR93a acts with the broadly expressed co-receptor IR25a.
source: In both of these roles, IR93a acts with the broadly expressed co-receptor IR25a.
evidence: This claim is supported by the co-expression and functional data presented.

claim: IR93a, IR25a, and a third distinct IR mediate thermosensation and hygrosensation in different populations of neurons.
source: However, these IRs mediate these two modalities in different populations of neurons in conjunction with a third, distinct IR: with IR21a in cool sensation, but not dry sensation, and with IR40a in dry sensation, but not cool sensation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the expression and functional data showing distinct IR combinations in different neurons.

claim: IR21a, IR25a, IR40a, and IR93a are widely conserved in insects.
source: All of these receptors are widely conserved in insects
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from comparative genomics.

claim: The IR-based sensory pathways likely underlie behavioral responses of diverse insect species to temperature and humidity.
source: indicating that these sensory pathways likely underlie behavioral responses of diverse species to these important environmental stimuli.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of these receptors across insects.

claim: The identification of an IR21a/IR25a/IR93a-dependent cool-sensing system provides a molecular counterpart to the well-established TRP channel and GR28B(D) warmth-sensing systems.
source: The identification of an IR21a/IR25a/IR93a-dependent cool-sensing system provides a molecular counterpart to the well-established TRP channel and 'Gustatory' Receptor GR28B(D) warmth-sensing systems (Barbagallo and Garrity, 2015; Ni et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to previously characterized thermosensory systems.

claim: Hygrosensation is important in helping insects to avoid desiccation or inundation.
source: By contrast, despite the importance of hygrosensation in helping insects to avoid desiccation or inundation (Chown et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work on insect ecology.

claim: Hygrosensation is important for blood-feeding species such as mosquitoes to locate mammalian hosts.
source: and – in blood-feeding species such as mosquitoes – to locate mammalian hosts (Brown, 1966; Olanga et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on mosquito behavior.

claim: The neuronal and molecular basis of hygrosensation is poorly understood.
source: the neuronal and molecular basis of this sensory modality is poorly understood.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of the state of the field.

claim: Hygrosensitive neurons have been identified electrophysiologically in large insects.
source: Hygrosensitive neurons have been identified electrophysiologically in large insects (Tichy and Gingl, 2001; Tichy and Kallina, 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous electrophysiological studies.

claim: The behavioral role of hygrosensitive neurons identified in large insects has been hard to determine.
source: but their behavioral role has been hard to determine.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of limitations in previous studies.

claim: The antenna has long been suspected to be an important hygrosensory organ in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, the antenna has long been suspected to be an important hygrosensory organ (Perttunen and Syrjamaki, 1958; Sayeed and Benzer, 1996)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: There has been little consensus on the relevant populations of neurons and sensory receptors for hygrosensation in Drosophila.
source: but there has been little consensus on the relevant populations of neurons and sensory receptors (Ji and Zhu, 2015; Liu et al., 2007; Yao et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to conflicting previous studies.

claim: A discrete population of dry-activated hygroreceptors in the sacculus express IR40a/IR93a/IR25a.
source: We have identified a discrete population of dry-activated hygroreceptors in the sacculus that express IR40a/IR93a/IR25a.
evidence: This claim is supported by the expression and physiological data presented.

claim: The data provide physiological and behavioral evidence supporting IR40a/IR93a/IR25a-expressing neurons as one pathway that enables flies to distinguish external humidity levels.
source: Together with an independent study (Enjin et al., 2016), our data provide physiological and behavioral evidence supporting these as one pathway that enables flies to distinguish external humidity levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented and comparison to an independent study.

claim: IR93a likely defines additional sensory pathways beyond cool and dry sensing.
source: In addition to the roles of IR93a in cool and dry sensing, it is very likely that this receptor defines additional sensory pathways.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on expression patterns.

claim: IR93a-positive cells that do not express IR21a or IR40a have been identified, such as non-DOCCs in the larval dorsal organ.
source: Our expression analysis has identified IR93a-positive cells that do not express IR21a or IR40a, such as non-DOCCs in the larval dorsal organ (Figure 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by expression data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The milder hygrosensory behavior phenotype of Ir40a mutants compared to Ir93a or Ir25a mutants hints that IR93a may have broader roles in hygrosensation than acting exclusively with IR40a.
source: Moreover, the milder hygrosensory behavior phenotype of our protein null Ir40a mutants compared to Ir93a (or Ir25a) mutants hints that IR93a may have broader roles in this sensory modality than acting exclusively with IR40a.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on comparison of mutant phenotypes.

claim: The populations of IR93a-expressing neurons characterized in this study are heterogeneous.
source: The populations of IR93a-expressing neurons characterized in this study are themselves heterogeneous.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing different properties of different IR93a-expressing populations.

claim: IR40a/IR93a/IR25a-expressing sacculus neurons belong to two morphologically and physiologically distinct subpopulations.
source: For example, IR40a/IR93a/IR25a-expressing sacculus neurons belong to two morphologically and physiologically distinct subpopulations.
evidence: This claim is based on the data and previous work showing distinct arm and column populations.

claim: Arm neurons have contralateral projections and respond robustly to low humidity.
source: Arm neurons have contralateral projections (Silbering et al., 2011) and respond robustly to low humidity
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented and citation to previous anatomical work.

claim: Column neurons are exclusively ipsilateral and respond more weakly to humidity.
source: while column neurons are exclusively ipsilateral (Silbering et al., 2011) and respond more weakly to humidity, as well as displaying mild thermosensitivity (Enjin et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: IR40a-expressing neurons also respond to ammonia.
source: IR40a-expressing neurons also respond to ammonia (Silbering et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: IR40a-expressing neurons are housed in apparently poreless sensilla.
source: Given that these neurons are housed in apparently poreless sensilla (Shanbhag et al., 1995)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous morphological work.

claim: Ammonia may activate IR40a-expressing neurons indirectly, for example through modification of the humidity of the air or the temperature of the cuticular surface within the sacculus.
source: we speculate that this chemical activates these cells indirectly, for example, through modification of the humidity of the air, or the temperature of the cuticular surface, within the sacculus.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the mechanism of ammonia detection.

claim: Ectopically-expressed IR21a can confer cool sensitivity to other IR-expressing neurons.
source: We previously showed that ectopically-expressed IR21a can confer cool sensitivity to other IR-expressing neurons, consistent with IR21a acting as a sensory specificity determinant (Ni et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: It will be important to determine if IR40a serves a more permissive role or functions in a similar capacity to IR21a in dry sensing.
source: It will be important to determine if IR40a serves a more permissive role or functions in a similar capacity in dry sensing.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: The contribution of the Venus flytrap-like ligand-binding domains of IRs to thermo- and hygrosensation is of particular interest.
source: The contribution (if any) of the Venus flytrap-like ligand-binding domains of these receptors is of particular interest.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: The Venus flytrap domain recognizes glutamate in iGluRs and diverse organic molecules in chemosensory IRs.
source: Although this domain recognizes glutamate in iGluRs, and diverse organic molecules in chemosensory IRs
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about iGluR and IR structure-function.

claim: It is conceivable that the Venus flytrap domains mediate thermo- and hygrosensory detection in these receptors in a ligand-independent manner.
source: it is conceivable that these domains mediate thermo- and hygrosensory detection in these receptors in a ligand-independent manner.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms.

claim: IR21a could transduce temperature information via temperature-dependent conformational changes.
source: For example, IR21a could transduce information via temperature-dependent conformational changes.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms.

claim: The requirement for IR93a and IR25a in both thermosensation and hygrosensation indicates that these modalities could share common mechanisms of sensory detection.
source: The requirement for IR93a (and IR25a) in both thermosensation and hygrosensation also indicates that these modalities could share common mechanisms of sensory detection.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the shared requirement for these receptors.

claim: Hygrosensation could involve a thermosensory component, based on evaporative cooling.
source: For example, hygrosensation could involve a thermosensory component, based on evaporative cooling.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms.

claim: Both temperature and moisture detection could involve mechanosensation, based on swelling or shrinkage of sensory structures, as suggested in mammals and C. elegans.
source: Alternatively, both temperature and moisture detection could involve mechanosensation, based on swelling or shrinkage of sensory structures, as suggested in mammals and C. elegans (Filingeri, 2015; Russell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on mechanisms proposed in other organisms.

claim: Thermosensory or hygrosensory responses cannot currently be reconstituted in heterologous systems by expressing the known combinations of IRs.
source: Further characterization of how IRs mediate temperature and moisture detection is currently limited by our inability to reconstitute thermosensory or hygrosensory responses in heterologous systems by expressing the known combinations of IRs (G.B., L.N., A.F.S., R.B. and P.G., unpublished data).
evidence: This claim is based on unpublished negative data from the authors.

claim: IRs are thought to form heterotetrameric complexes like iGluRs.
source: IRs, like iGluRs, are thought to form heterotetrameric complexes (Abuin et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work on IR structure.

claim: Additional IR subunits may be required for thermosensory or hygrosensory responses.
source: raising the possibility that additional IR subunits are required.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about why heterologous expression has not been successful.

claim: Other types of accessory signaling molecules may act with IRs in thermosensation and hygrosensation.
source: It is also conceivable that other types of accessory signaling molecules act with IRs
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms.

claim: The cellular and cuticular specializations of the thermosensory and hygrosensory structures may be critical to allow monitoring of temperature and humidity.
source: and/or that the cellular and cuticular specializations of the thermosensory and hygrosensory structures are critical to allow monitoring of these ubiquitous and ever-changing environmental stimuli.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms.

claim: The sacculus is a three-chambered pouch whose opening lies on the posterior surface of the antenna.
source: the sacculus, a three-chambered pouch whose opening lies on the posterior surface of the antenna
evidence: This claim is based on established anatomical knowledge and illustrated in Figure 3a.

claim: The dorsal organ is one of the main sensory organs in the larval head.
source: the dorsal organ ganglion, one of the main sensory organs in the larval head (Stocker, 1994)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous anatomical work.

claim: The hygrosensory behavior assay created a humidity gradient of ~96% relative humidity (RH) to ~67% RH, with negligible variation in temperature.
